stages.title: Focused application: the application-handle route
stages.summary: WMS publishes an ActivityRecord's InputApplicationHandle through InputManagerService and JNI. InputDispatcher tracks that application independently of any focused window. These excerpts describe the local checkout, not a version-independent Android contract.

snippets.note: Changing the focused ActivityRecord publishes an application handle; it does not establish an input-window focus token. Omitted code validates the display and updates task bookkeeping.
The focused-application update carries an InputApplicationHandle, not an input-channel token.
Java forwards this update to its native implementation, separately from SurfaceControl focus transactions.

Current-checkout caveat: a null Java application handle returns here. Do not claim that Java setFocusedApplication(null) reaches InputDispatcher to clear its map or reset its timer. A direct native dispatcher call has different behavior.
A changed application handle resets the current wait. Merely setting an application does not arm a no-focused-window timer; an unchanged handle returns without resetting.

stages.title: Focused window: the transaction and window-info route
stages.summary: Window focus is requested with an input-channel token in a SurfaceControl transaction. SurfaceFlinger sends window information and focus requests from BackgroundExecutor; InputDispatcher resolves the request against its window information. WMS having requested focus does not prove native input focus has taken effect.

snippets.note: mInputFocus and mInputFocusRequestTimeMillis describe WMS's request. They are not an acknowledgement that FocusResolver has granted native focus.
The normal non-immediate path merges the input transaction into the display's pending transaction and schedules animation. This is not an immediate native focus update.

The callback's executor is BackgroundExecutor, not the WMS caller or SurfaceFlinger's main-thread caller. The excerpt establishes send order, not a universal acknowledgement or presentation guarantee.
A focus request is resolved against the native window handles for its display. The request token alone does not establish focus.
Window-info updates also drive resolution. The omitted code validates the update, groups windows by display, and acquires the dispatcher lock.
setInputWindowsLocked re-evaluates the pending focus request after updating window handles. Focus can therefore become effective after the original request arrives.

stages.title: FocusResolver: a requested window must qualify
stages.summary: A request can remain pending while the native window is missing, not focusable, or not visible. FocusResolver stores the request and can remove old focus until a suitable window becomes available. It also supports focus-transfer targets; this is not simply a first-draw callback test.

snippets.note: WMS itself can defer issuing the request when there is no surface or its input-window handle is not focusable. This predicate is separate from the native resolver's eligibility checks.
The omitted success branch grants focus to the resolved token. The shown final return is the failure path, not an unconditional removal of focus for every request.
For a token with multiple native windows, at least one must be visible and all matching windows must be focusable. A visible surface or completed app drawing alone is not proof of input focus.

stages.title: Key and non-pointer events need focus; pointers use hit testing
stages.summary: The no-focused-window path is entered when a focus-dependent event actually reaches target selection. Keys can first be consumed or delayed by policy. Pointer motion uses touched-window targeting instead; neither an arbitrary input event nor an idle unfocused application automatically arms this timer.

snippets.note: In dispatchKeyLocked, PENDING returns false, so this event has not completed dispatch. Earlier policy interception/drop paths can avoid target lookup entirely.

This is dispatchMotionLocked's source-class split, not a split between every MotionEvent and every KeyEvent. Pointer events can still cause a separate delivered-event/ACK timeout; they do not arm this focus-wait timer through this branch.
Both handles missing causes FAILED/drop, not an ANR against an arbitrary application. Application and window lookups use the event's resolved display.

stages.title: Arm the current state and leave the event pending
stages.summary: At the first target lookup with an application but no focused window, the deadline is currentTime plus the application's dispatch timeout. The state stores the original entry.eventTime separately. The timer does not start at Activity launch, onResume, first draw, or at the original input timestamp.

snippets.code:
void InputDispatcher::dispatchOnceInnerLocked(nsecs_t& nextWakeupTime) {
    nsecs_t currentTime = now();
snippets.note: The currentTime passed through dispatch and target selection is the dispatch iteration's sampled monotonic time, not entry.eventTime.

This is the active implementation. Do not substitute the old mNoFocusedWindowTimeoutTime/mAwaitedFocusedApplication fields from docs/ANR. eventTime is diagnostic input metadata, not the deadline's origin. There is one optional wait state in this dispatcher, plus the awaited display ID.

Repeated target lookups while this state exists do not extend its deadline. This branch uses > for event dropping; the actual processAnrsLocked timeout decision uses >=. The comment is not proof that the policy callback already ran.
A false/done-not-complete result preserves mPendingEvent. This is a wait before selecting/delivering an application target, not a missing finishInputEvent acknowledgement from this event.

stages.title: Feature-gated pre-ANR warning, not the full ANR gate
stages.summary: enable_anr_warning_callback_input_dispatcher gates only the early warning path. Its scheduled point is deadline - max(timeoutDuration / 2, 2000 ms * HW multiplier). For a 5000 ms timeout and multiplier 1 this is 2500 ms after arming, not a fixed 2000 ms delay. Small configured timeouts can put this warning point before the arming time.

snippets.note: The member is initialized from the feature flag. Source inspection alone does not establish a device's generated flag value.
Disabling warnings does not disable processAnrsLocked or full no-focused-window ANRs.

At most one warning is queued per wait state. elapsed is calculated from the deadline and configured duration, not from entry.eventTime. A scheduled warning is not a hard real-time callback guarantee.
Warning delivery is queued and invokes policy with the dispatcher lock released. It neither resets nor extends the full ANR deadline.

WMS warning handling drops unknown/stopped activities. Long-method tracing has a separate enableInputDispatcherLongMethodTracing flag; the warning does not enter the full notifyAppUnresponsive path here.

stages.title: Deadline expiry and the native final state check
stages.summary: The dispatch loop checks full ANRs independently of the warning flag. At currentTime >= timeoutEndTime, native code rechecks that the awaited application token is still focused on the awaited display and that there is still no focused window. It then queues a policy callback and clears the wait state.

snippets.note: Both functions are evaluated. The warning flag check is inside processPreAnrsLocked, not a gate around processAnrsLocked.
The no-focus deadline is checked directly rather than being an AnrTracker entry for a connection's waitQueue. Clearing the state after this check is housekeeping, not proof that no ANR was reported.

The application comparison is token identity, not shared-pointer equality. A non-null focused window suppresses this report without a further same-application ownership comparison. The omitted mismatch logging dereferences focusedApplication even in the null branch; do not treat that exceptional branch as proven crash-safe behavior.
The loop polls until its next wakeup/deadline or another wake event. Timeout eligibility, queued callback execution, stack collection, and a visible ANR dialog are different moments.

stages.title: Reset entry points and cancellation limits
stages.summary: Current cpp calls reset when target selection finds a focused window, the native focused application changes, a new focus is granted, dispatch is unfrozen, all dispatch state is dropped, and the deadline has been processed. Pointer-down pruning and releasing mPendingEvent are not direct reset calls. A reset cannot retract an already captured policy command.

snippets.note: A new focus event preserves the pending event by re-enqueueing it. Clearing A's wait does not by itself discard the key. The switch scenario selects a ready B window without touch-driven pruning.
A touch-driven unblock can separately mark a preceding key BLOCKED. This requires mNextUnblockedEvent; it must not be inferred from the focused application merely changing.
Reset clears the consolidated state, including its one-warning-per-state bit. It does not operate on the legacy timeout field that remains declared in the header.

snippets.code:
// we have a valid, non-null focused window
    resetNoFocusedWindowTimeoutLocked();
snippets.note: findFocusedWindowTargetLocked resets the wait once it finds an actual focused window, before later injection, paused-dispatch, and previous-event checks.
setFocusedApplicationLocked reaches this reset after updating its map for a changed handle. The Java/JNI null early return remains a separate caveat.
onFocusChangedLocked resets when native resolution grants a non-null new focus. Sending a WMS request or app onWindowFocusChanged callback is not the reset predicate.
setInputDispatchMode resets on unfreezing. Disabling dispatch instead invokes the reset/drop-everything path. Do not infer a reset from every mode setter call.
This explicitly resets both the no-focus wait and the separate connection ANR tracking. releasePendingEventLocked alone does not perform this combined reset.
This reset happens after the final expiry check and may happen after onAnrLocked has captured the report into a queued command. It is not a cancellation of that command.

Touching another application can unblock/prune preceding events, but this const helper does not reset the timer. Do not animate every touch as an immediate cancellation; the relevant subsequent focus/app/reset transition must actually occur.

stages.title: Queued policy callback crosses JNI into WMS
stages.summary: The native expiry handler snapshots application/event/timeout metadata into a command. The command releases the dispatcher lock before calling policy, then JNI enters InputManagerService, which creates an input-dispatch-no-focused-window TimeoutRecord and forwards it through InputManagerCallback to WMS AnrController.

snippets.note: This is the application-handle overload, not the unresponsive-connection overload. The captured eventTime remains the input event's original timestamp; duration is the configured no-focus threshold.
This native-to-Java callback is a JNI CallVoidMethod, not a Binder call into the application and not the app's main-thread event handler.
includeAnrInfo controls enrichment of the record, not whether this callback is forwarded. The standardized reason is Application does not have a focused window.
WMS receives an application handle and TimeoutRecord, then performs its own state and attribution checks. Native timeout detection is not the final dialog decision.

stages.title: WMS rechecks activity state, focus-request age, and recovery
stages.summary: WMS drops an unknown or mAppStopped activity. An old enough pending focus request can redirect blame to its target window, which need not belong to the awaited application. Otherwise ActivityRecord forwards the timeout to AMS. There is no explicit requirement that the ActivityRecord be in RESUMED state in notifyAppUnresponsive. inputDispatchingResumed is a later recovery notification, not that lifecycle predicate.

snippets.note: These checks run under the WMS global lock. Do not replace mAppStopped with an invented isState(RESUMED) gate, or assert that onResume completion implies native window focus.

This checks the age of WMS's requested focus against the target activity's dispatch timeout. It is attribution for a lagging/pending focus request, not proof of an app main-thread deadlock, an SF defect, or an additional full-timeout waiting period.

A successful pending-window attribution calls the window path; otherwise the ActivityRecord path is used. Only the non-pending-window-blame branch shown here records the activity for focus-based recovery.

For the ordinary no-focus path, INVALID_PID allows attribution to the ActivityRecord's process when it exists. Other branches can use the generic window-PID route; not every callback guarantees an available process.
This downstream historical-attribution helper can consult a top resumed or pausing activity when stopped. It is not an upfront RESUMED prerequisite in WMS's no-focus callback.

AMS has further process/debugger/instrumentation handling before normal AnrHelper processing. This evidence does not establish that every native timeout produces a dialog, kills the app, or identifies a blocked main thread.

Recovery requires the newly focused window to belong to the recorded unresponsive activity on that display. This runs after reporting; it is not the native timer's reset predicate or an Activity lifecycle resumed check.
Here the resumed notification requests dismissal of the process's ANR dialogs. It does not prove the earlier timeout never happened or cancel every already queued ANR task.

stages.title: Default 5000 ms, HW multiplier, and application overrides
stages.summary: The base default is 5000 ms multiplied by the hardware timeout multiplier. The pre-ANR lead window's base is 2000 ms with the same multiplier. No-focused-window waiting uses the application's configured dispatch timeout when its handle has a token; the default is a fallback, not an unconditional five-second constant.

snippets.note: These are base constants. The device property value and actual generated feature-flag values were not measured by this source investigation.
Use the executable pre-ANR formula from processNoFocusedWindowPreAnrLocked: this constant is its minimum warning lead window, not always the time elapsed since arming.
The Java default is already multiplied; do not multiply the configured application timeout again in a model.
A valid application token selects its supplied dispatchingTimeoutMillis. The native default does not override that configured value and is not multiplied into it here.
Instrumentation or a wrapper selects a different configured timeout. Do not generalize the ordinary default to every process.

snippets.code: static final long INSTRUMENTATION_KEY_DISPATCHING_TIMEOUT_MILLIS = 60 * 1000;
snippets.note: The instrumentation/wrapper branch above selects 60000 ms in this checkout; this expression itself does not apply the HW multiplier.
Process attachment updates the ActivityRecord's configured input timeout. A model must treat configuration and the already-armed state's snapshotted duration as separate values.

The configured ActivityRecord timeout is carried into the application handle published by setFocusedAppLw. Updating configuration is not evidence that an existing native deadline is extended in place.
